So, again there is no difference between the time for the recursive and iterative versions
except that one should keep in mind in general that recursive calls are more expensive than
iterative loops.
We will come back to this point a little later.
But otherwise if we count recursive calls calling a function as a basic operation then
there is no difference between the recursive and the iterative versions.
The recursive version is sometimes easier to conceptually understand and to call.
So, what we have seen is that the two natural algorithms that we would typically apply
when we do something manually selection sort and insertion sort are both order n square.
There is another algorithm which you may come across which we will not discuss in this course
called bubble sort which is not something that we would do naturally but it seems to be
a favorite way of describing how to do things on a computer.
So, bubble sort basically takes does this insertion kind of swapping except it takes the maximum
of the minimum value depending on which you want to do.
Say it takes the maximum value and moves it to one end of the array.
So, then you have like selection sort the largest value at one end.
Then you go back to the beginning and again you keep looking at adjacent values and take
the second largest value to the second last position and so on.
So, bubble sort is also n square but as we have seen n square algorithms are not really
feasible for large values of n.
So, if we have n above about 10,000 somewhere between 10 to the 4 and 10 to the 5 then n square
is going to take several hundred seconds to execute and therefore, this is not going
to be useful for large bodies of data.
But this is not to say that these algorithms are all equally bad in particular it turns
out that if you actually look at experimental evidence then an insertion sort usually behaves
better than selection sort and both of them are better than bubble sort.
And to think about why insertion sort behaves well just imagine what happens when we apply
insertion sort to an already sorted list.
So, whenever we want to sort some insert something into the already sorted list we will
find that it is already in the correct position.
So, the bottleneck which is the insert phase is the bottleneck.
The insert phase will basically terminate after one one comparison.
So, insertion sort will essentially become linear time if we apply it to an already sorted
list.
So, this is why in many situations insertion sort actually behaves a little better than
other order n square source.
But in general order n square sorting algorithms are not acceptable and we would like to look
